# Independent audit: continuous minimal maximal depth and simplex rigidity

Audited `candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c` in full.
Result: PASS for its ordinary continuous classification and compact
stability statement. No correction is required. The proof uses no
mixed-integer extremal assertion.

## 1. External equality input and orientation

I independently opened the primary source cited in the note:
[Tanganelli Castrillon, An improved stability result for Grunbaum's
inequality](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12072v2), Introduction,
equation (1.1) and its following paragraph. It records that centroid-cap
equality characterizes a cone with the cutting plane parallel to its
base. The cone convention there is the compact convex hull of an apex
and a hyperplanar base. No stability theorem from that paper is used
by the audited classification.

For d>=2 the equality side is necessarily the apex side: its fraction
is gamma_d<1/2, whereas the opposite side has fraction 1-gamma_d.
The normalized affine height lambda, zero on the base and one at the
apex, therefore has gradient a POSITIVE multiple of the inward cap
normal and mean 1/(d+1). Direct integration of the profile
(1-t)^(d-1) proves that mean and removes any orientation ambiguity.
Dimension one is handled separately as an interval.

## 2. Active centroid normals really balance

At D(K)=gamma_d, ordinary Grunbaum and compactness of the unit sphere
give a nonempty compact family U of equality caps at the centroid g.
If zero is outside conv(U), strict separation gives v with u.v>=a>0
on U and u.v>=a/2 on a neighborhood. Moving the point to g-tv moves
the through-cap threshold DOWN in each such direction, so every one
of those caps gains volume. This sign is correct.

For an inner ball g+rB subset K, all sections within distance r/2 of
g have (d-1)-volume at least the section volume of that ball at r/2.
Integrating over the added slab gives a uniform positive gain times t.
An enclosing ball bounds every section from above, uniformly in the
normal, so all other caps lose at most O(t). On the compact complement
of the chosen neighborhood their original excess is uniformly positive.
For sufficiently small t every cap exceeds gamma_d, a contradiction.
This argument needs neither a differentiable body boundary nor
differentiability of the depth function.

Caratheodory therefore gives at most d+1 distinct unit normals with
strictly positive balancing weights after zero weights are discarded.

## 3. Repeated apex issue and height identities

For any pyramid K=conv(v,F), every extreme point other than v belongs
to F. Conversely, each extreme point of F is extreme in K, because F
is an exposed face. The extreme points of the (d-1)-dimensional convex
body F affinely span its whole supporting hyperplane. Thus if a second
pyramid representation had the SAME apex v, all other extreme points
would force exactly the SAME base hyperplane. Its oriented unit normal
is uniquely determined by the apex side. Distinct selected normals
therefore have distinct apices. This remains valid when F has infinitely
many extreme points; no polytope hypothesis is hidden here.

For the distinct apices v_i, the corresponding height functions satisfy
lambda_i(v_j)=delta_ij. Rescale the positive normal balance to
sum beta_i grad(lambda_i)=0, with all beta_i>0. The affine function
sum beta_i lambda_i is a constant h. Evaluation at each v_j gives
beta_j=h, so h>0 and sum lambda_i=1 everywhere. Integration now gives
k/(d+1)=1, hence k=d+1.

The Kronecker evaluation equations make these d+1 apices affinely
independent: an affine dependence is annihilated coefficient by
coefficient by the lambda_i. They are the barycentric functions of
their simplex. Their nonnegativity on K and sum one imply K is contained
in that simplex, while the reverse inclusion follows from its vertices
lying in K. This establishes the forward implication completely.
The converse facet-parallel cap volume (1-lambda_i(y))^d is correct,
including a boundary point with zero cap volume.

## 4. Depth continuity and the compact stability gap

Full-dimensional uniform volume gives each hyperplane zero mass, so
the cap function is jointly continuous in normal and point on compact
parameter sets. Sphere minimization preserves continuity. Exterior and
boundary points have depth zero, whereas the centroid has positive
depth, so the maximum is attained in the body's interior.

For normalized measures, the inequality

    |D(mu)-D(nu)|<=sup_A|mu(A)-nu(A)|

holds without restrictions on optimizing points: first take infima
of halfspace masses at each fixed point, then suprema over all points.
Hausdorff convergence between B and RB gives almost-everywhere
indicator convergence and L1 convergence, since the full-dimensional
limiting boundary is null. Positive volumes also converge, giving
total-variation convergence after normalization. Hence D is continuous
on that body class.

The hulls of d+1 points in RB form a compact family when degenerate
hulls are included. Distance from this family is continuous, and the
epsilon-separated body class is compact. A zero minimum gap there
would, by attainment and the proved classification, be a simplex in
the forbidden family. Therefore the attained gap is strictly positive.
Equivalently one can phrase the hypothesis using only nondegenerate
simplices: these are dense in the compact family of possibly degenerate
hulls, by arbitrarily small perturbations of their vertices inside RB.

This supplies an unspecified positive modulus for fixed d,R,epsilon.
It does not supply a rate, a dimension-uniform gap, or an assertion
about mixed-volume sources or extracted mixed extremizers.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
